passage: Suraj, put that packet down a moment and listen. I'm Wasim, your grandfather, and I once believed a poster too. I was ten. A film wrestler on a biscuit tin said the biscuits made you strong like him, and I ate them for a month, flexing at the mirror. Nothing changed, except that my pocket money vanished. Finally I asked my father, "Does this really make me strong?" He laughed kindly and read the back of the tin with me. He said the poster was there to sell tins. "Ask before you believe," he told me. So ask your mother about that packet with the cartoon lion, beta. She may say yes, she may say no, but you will know more.

qa.q: How long did Wasim eat the biscuits?
qa.a: He ate them for a month.

qa.q: Why did ten-year-old Wasim keep eating the biscuits?
qa.a: He believed the wrestler on the tin when it said the biscuits made you strong.

qa.q: What could Suraj do about the packet with the cartoon lion?
qa.a: Ask Suraj's mother whether the snack is really good before believing the cartoon, as Wasim suggests.

qa.q: How did Wasim's father react when he asked if the biscuits made him strong?
qa.a: He laughed kindly and read the back of the tin with him, explaining that the poster was there to sell tins.

grounding: A child believes an ad's claim about a snack making him strong and learns to ask a parent whether it is true.

passage:
Monday: On TV, a cartoon lion lifted a bus after one bowl of Zoom Flakes. "Eat Zoom Flakes, be strong!" Deepika decided that was why she kept losing arm-wrestling to her friend Dolma.
Wednesday: At the supermarket, Deepika dropped the bright box into the trolley. "Mummy, I need it to get strong."
Mummy turned the box over. "Who made this ad, do you think?"
"The lion?"
"The company that sells the cereal. They want you to buy it. Let's ask the doctor on Friday whether it really makes children strong."
Friday: At Deepika's check-up, the doctor laughed kindly. "Lions don't eat cereal. Playing, sleeping well and ordinary home food do the job."
Saturday: Deepika arm-wrestled Dolma again, lost again, and giggled anyway.

qa.q: What did the cartoon lion lift in the ad?
Why did Deepika want the cereal so badly?
qa.a: She believed the ad and felt hopeful it would make her strong enough to beat Dolma.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that helped Deepika understand the ad?
qa.a: She asked who made the ad, explained that the company wants to sell, and suggested asking the doctor.

qa.q: What does the company behind the ad want children like Deepika to believe?
qa.a: That the cereal will make them strong, so they will beg their parents to buy it.

grounding: A girl believes a cartoon ad that a cereal makes you strong and learns, by asking a parent, that ads are made to sell.

passage: Imran, you want that energy drink because the cricketer on TV says it makes you hit sixes? Sit, let your Kavitha Aunty tell you something. When I was a girl, a famous film heroine was in a malt-drink ad. She said, "One glass a day and you'll shine like me!" I believed every word. I cried until Appa bought a tin. I drank it every morning and looked in the mirror every evening. No shine. One day Appa asked, "Kavitha, who pays the heroine to say that?" I thought hard. "The company?" "Yes. She is selling, not advising." I felt so silly, and a bit cheated. After that, whenever an ad promised magic, I asked Appa or my teacher whether it was true. Now go and ask your Ammi about that drink, Imran.

qa.q: What did the heroine in the ad promise?
qa.a: That one glass a day would make you shine like her.

qa.q: How did young Kavitha feel when she understood the heroine was paid?
qa.a: She felt silly and a bit cheated for believing every word.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Aunty's story?
qa.a: Appa's question about who pays the heroine, which helped her see ads sell things and start checking with adults.

qa.q: How might Appa have seen young Kavitha crying for the tin?
qa.a: He probably saw an ad pulling his daughter in, so he bought it once and later asked a question to help her think.

grounding: An aunty recalls believing a celebrity ad as a child and learning, with a parent's help, that ads sell rather than advise.
